Summary:
Quick discovery with EmberWave to understand their cost sensitivity for running inference across hosted, dedicated and private deployments. Focus on per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, and a tight budget cap for Q1 pilot. They have strict SSO + KMS requirements and want to see tradeoffs for latency vs unit cost (esp for RAG and chat endpoints).

Topics: per-token economics, batching/caching, burst capacity, VPC/private options, SOC2/KMS, pilot scope and timeline

--- Transcript ---
[15:30] Alex Martinez (AE, Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick intro from our side, I'm Alex, I'm the AE, Priya's our solutions engineer. Who do we have on from EmberWave?
[15:31] Tom Hale (CTO, EmberWave): Hi Alex, Tom here. Sara Lin, Head of ML, Javier our infra lead and Rina product. We're mostly focused on cost, we ran some back-of-envelope budget targets and, uh, want clarity on how Redwood's levers map to our unit economics.
[15:31] Alex Martinez: Great. high level, can you give a short sense of expected workload? e.g., avg tokens per request, mix of embedding vs chat vs RAG?
[15:32] Sara Lin (Head of ML): Sure. Most traffic is chat-like, average 250 tokens in prompt with 150 generated on average per call. We also have a small batch of embeddings for similarity (0.5k calls/day). Peak concurrent chat RPS is around 12, sustained 3-4 RPS. Budget target for pilot is $6k/month for inference.
[15:32] Priya Desai (SE, Redwood): OK thanks. that budget is pretty tight for a chat workload with that generation length. Couple of levers we typically look at: batching, prefix/KV caching for repeated context, quantized model variants, and routing between hosted/dedicated/private to balance cost SLOs.
[15:33] Tom Hale: Could you give concrete per-token numbers? we tried to do simple multiply but there's so many variables.
[15:33] Alex Martinez: Absolutely. for example, on Redwood Hosted with our mid-sized open model family, the nominal list price is roughly $0.000015 per input token and $0.00003 per output token for that model class — but that's a baseline. With caching and batching for interactive sessions you can reduce effective per-token to maybe 30-60% depending on prefix reuse and how much batching you tolerate for latency.
[15:34] Javier Ortiz (Infra): That $0.00003/out token, how does that change if we go Dedicated? we prefer reserved capacity if it cuts unit costs.
[15:34] Priya Desai: On Dedicated you get committed capacity discounts; typical committed deals we've done show unit costs drop 40-60% vs hosted list, but you trade off flexibility and you need a commit. For your scale, a small dedicated pool could be cost-effective if you have steady sustained throughput in business hours. Also Dedicated lets you pin a quantized variant which reduces GPU memory and cost.
[15:35] Sara Lin: What about Private (VPC) — our legal likes that but I'm worried about ops overhead.
[15:35] Alex Martinez: Private adds platform fee and some ops overhead; per-token raw compute is similar to Dedicated if you're running same nodes, but the package cost (support, network egress, setup) is higher. Usually customers go Private when they need data residency or HSM/KMS integration — you mentioned KMS earlier?
[15:35] Rina Patel (Product): yes, our security team requires customer-managed keys and audit trails. SOC2 a must.
[15:36] Priya Desai: We support KMS/HSM integration for Private and Dedicated, plus audit logs and RBAC. For Hosted we have SOC2 and we offer tenant-level audit logs; if you need customer-managed keys and a private control plane, that's Private. There's an onboarding timeline to consider.
[15:36] Tom Hale: Back to cost math — you mentioned caching. our product has many repeated prompts and system messages; would that help?
[15:37] Priya Desai: Yes, prefix/KV caching helps a lot for chat with repeated system prompts and long context windows. If you can cache the KV for the conversation start you avoid re-computing large portions of attention, which reduces per-request GPU cycles. In practice we've seen effective token cost reductions of 25-50% for long-conversation RAG/chat when caching works well.
[15:37] Sara Lin: How invasive is it to enable? we don't want app-level changes.
[15:38] Priya Desai: We have client-side and server-side options. Client-side small change to how you call the streaming APIs and attach conversation IDs; server-side has more automation but may need session pinning. We'll share a runbook.
[15:38] [15:38] Speaker 5: (mumble) question on quotas — what happens if we exceed reserved capacity?
[15:38] Alex Martinez: Good question. on Dedicated you can configure burst capacity or automatic fallback to hosted. Fallback means slightly higher unit cost but keeps availability. You can set policy: fail fast, queue, or fallback.
[15:39] Javier Ortiz: Let's talk latency tradeoffs. our UX needs median < 400ms for small prompts, but long completions can be slower.
[15:39] Priya Desai: Batching increases throughput and reduces token cost, but adds tail latency. We use continuous batching where latency SLOs are prioritized and small requests pass quickly, larger requests may batch. For your median target we would recommend small batch windows (10-20ms) and aggressive KV caching to keep token compute lower.
[15:40] Tom Hale: Give me an example: with our 250+150 tokens, what's expected average latency and monthly cost on Hosted vs Dedicated?
[15:40] Alex Martinez: Rough sketch: Hosted (baseline) — assuming no caching and low batching: 400-800ms median for that size, cost approx: (250 in * 0.000015) + (150 out * 0.00003) = 0.00375 + 0.0045 = $0.00825 per call. At 10k calls/month that's $82.50. But if you have sustained RPS and use batching + caching, effective per-call could drop ~35% -> ~ $0.0054 per call. Dedicated might get you down to $0.003 - $0.004 per call depending on commit and quantization. Those are rough numbers — we'll send a model spread.
[15:41] Sara Lin: Wait, your $0.00825 baseline seems low relative to our estimates. Are you sure? we ran some numbers that double that.
[15:41] Alex Martinez: Good catch — depends on the model family and sequence length tail. I used a mid-tier open model example. If you pick a higher-capability variant per-token is higher. Also streaming tokens charged as they emit, and you have tokenization differences. We'll run the exact model and tokenization on your prompt set.
[15:41] Rina Patel: How do discounts work if we do a 12-month commit? we have a roadmap to scale fast.
[15:42] Priya Desai: Commit pricing usually gives 20-50% off list depending on term and size. For pilots, we often do a 90-day committed pilot with an option to convert. We can propose a pilot SOW that has clear unit economic targets and a convert clause.
[15:42] Tom Hale: Regarding billing visibility, we need token-level breakdown per route and per user.
[15:42] Alex Martinez: Redwood Console provides token-level cost (input/output), per-model, per-route dashboards, and you can set alerts. We'll give you a demo link.
[15:43] Javier Ortiz: Network egress and VPC costs — will that be on top?
[15:43] Priya Desai: For Hosted, egress is not usually a major line item unless you're moving huge attachments. For Private or on-prem, network setup and egress may be part of the infra cost. We'll annotate that in the pricing scenarios.
[15:44] Speaker label glitch (transcript): Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[15:44] Tom Hale: Security checklist: SSO/SAML, KMS, SOC2, ability to restrict data retention. Are those supported?
[15:44] Alex Martinez: Yes. Hosted supports SSO, retention settings, and SOC2. For customer-managed keys and full control you need Private or some Dedicated packages. We have an SOC2 pack and an audit doc we can share.
[15:45] Sara Lin: For pilot success criteria we want: 1) cost per active user below X (they didn't give X), 2) median latency under 500ms for typical chat, 3) no data exfil with KMS enforced, 4) minimal engineering effort to integrate.
[15:45] Rina Patel: Also need an exec-friendly ROI slide showing break-even vs self-hosting.
[15:46] Priya Desai: We'll build a short ROI comparison: Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, factoring commit discounts, ops effort, and infra TCO. We'll include sensitivity to cache hit rate and batch windows.
[15:46] Tom Hale: What about model variants and quantization compatibility? we have some proprietary fine-tuning.
[15:46] Marco Li (Solutions Eng): We support many quantization profiles; some fine-tuned weights need per-model validation. If you want to bring a fine-tuned checkpoint for Private or Dedicated, we'll run a compatibility and perf sweep. For Hosted we can host vetted variants where licensing allows.
[15:47] Sara Lin: Can you do a quick sketch of a pilot plan so we can review with legal and security?
[15:47] Alex Martinez: Outline: 90-day pilot, sample prompt set, Redwood hosts pilot on Hosted with optional Dedicated reserve if numbers justify, include KV caching config and 2-week perf benchmark, security review within first 10 days, SOW and pricing scenarios by 2026-12-18, kickoff last week of December.
[15:48] Tom Hale: That timeline should work for us. we'll try to get prompt sets and traffic profile by the 20th.
[15:48] Alex Martinez: Great. any other questions?
[15:48] Sara Lin: One minor nit — when you send the benchmark sheet, include an example of how caching might look in our logs so we can show security.
[15:49] Priya Desai: Will do, include sample logs and redaction guidance.
[15:49] Rina Patel: Also need a short note on data residency and retention policy for Hosted — what are default retention windows?
[15:49] Alex Martinez: Default retention is 30 days for non-PII telemetry; we can configure to shorter windows. We'll include that in the security pack.
